Omri
OM-ree
proper noun (figure)
Hebrew Omri (H6018) — possibly "life" or "servant of Yahweh"; uncertain. The Assyrian and Moabite inscriptions transliterate the name Humri or Khumri, and for centuries afterward the Assyrian royal annals referred to the northern kingdom as "the house of Omri" (Bit-Humri) even after his dynasty had fallen — testimony to his political-military weight in international affairs.

Biblical Definition

Omri (c. 885 — 874 BC) was the sixth king of the northern kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 16:15-28), founder of the Omride dynasty, builder of the capital city of Samaria, father of the notorious Ahab, and one of the most internationally significant kings of the divided monarchy — almost universally treated in extrabiblical Assyrian and Moabite sources but dispatched in only fourteen verses by the canonical record because his doctrinal record was so wicked. He rose to power as a military commander when his predecessor Zimri assassinated King Elah and seized the throne for seven days (1 Kings 16:9-15); the army at Gibbethon proclaimed Omri king instead, who marched on Tirzah, took the city, and watched Zimri burn the palace down around himself rather than be captured. For four years thereafter Omri fought a civil war against a rival claimant, Tibni son of Ginath, finally prevailing in the field. He then made the political-geographic decision that defined the remaining history of the northern kingdom: he bought the hill of Shomron (Samaria) from a man named Shemer for two talents of silver and built a new capital there (1 Kings 16:24). Samaria became the seat of Israel's monarchy until its fall to Assyria in 722 BC, and the name passed to the surrounding region ("the country of the Samaritans") and to the post-exilic Samaritans of New Testament times (John 4). The canonical verdict is severe: "Omri wrought evil in the eyes of the LORD, and did worse than all that were before him" (1 Kings 16:25). His son Ahab and grandson Joram continued the dynasty in the same wicked pattern; his daughter Athaliah carried the Omride apostasy south by marriage into the Davidic house and almost destroyed it. Micah 6:16 specifically denounces "the statutes of Omri" as a continuing snare to Israel a century after his death.

Webster 1828 Definition

Sixth king of the northern kingdom of Israel (c. 885-874 BC); founder of the Omride dynasty; built the capital of Samaria; father of Ahab; called 'worse than all that were before him' (1 Kings 16:25); the international Assyrian annals continued to call Israel 'the house of Omri' for centuries.

OMRI, proper noun. Hebrew Omri (H6018); uncertain meaning; possibly "life" or "servant of Yahweh." Assyrian and Moabite sources transliterate Humri/Khumri.

Sixth king of the divided northern kingdom of Israel (c. 885-874 BC); founder of the Omride dynasty.

Built the capital city of Samaria on a hill bought from Shemer for two talents of silver (1 Kings 16:24); the city remained Israel's capital until 722 BC.

Father of Ahab; grandfather of Joram; great-uncle (through Athaliah's marriage to Jehoram of Judah) of the Judahite Ahaziah; the Omride dynasty's apostasy poisoned both kingdoms for a generation.

Mentioned in extrabiblical sources: Mesha Stele (Moabite), Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III (Assyrian), royal annals of Tiglath-Pileser III (Assyrian).

Key Scripture

1 Kings 16:23-24 — "In the thirty and first year of Asa king of Judah began Omri to reign over Israel, twelve years: six years reigned he in Tirzah. And he bought the hill Samaria of Shemer for two talents of silver, and built on the hill, and called the name of the city which he built, after the name of Shemer, owner of the hill, Samaria."

1 Kings 16:25-26 — "But Omri wrought evil in the eyes of the LORD, and did worse than all that were before him. For he walked in all the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and in his sin wherewith he made Israel to sin."

Micah 6:16 — "For the statutes of Omri are kept, and all the works of the house of Ahab, and ye walk in their counsels; that I should make thee a desolation, and the inhabitants thereof an hissing."

Joshua 13:1-2 — "Now Joshua was old and stricken in years; and the LORD said unto him, Thou art old and stricken in years, and there remaineth yet very much land to be possessed."

Modern Corruption

Omri is corrupted when his international political-military significance is read as positive achievement rather than as canon's deliberately understated record of a wicked king, when the building of Samaria is treated as urban-planning success rather than as the symbol of northern apostasy it became, or when his statutes (Mic 6:16) are read merely historically without their continuing covenant-warning weight.

expand to see more

Political-success-as-canonical-praise. Omri was clearly successful by the metrics of ancient Near Eastern statecraft: he ended a civil war, founded a long-lived capital city, established a dynasty that lasted three generations (until Jehu's coup), and made the northern kingdom internationally consequential enough that Assyria continued to refer to Israel as 'the house of Omri' for two centuries after his death. The canonical record allots him fourteen verses and a damning verdict. Modern Near-Eastern-history readings sometimes flip this proportion and treat the Bible's reticence as a curious gap. The Chronicler's logic is theological: political success without covenant fidelity is not worth more space; the LORD's people need to know that Omri did worse than all before him, not how many talents of silver he weighed out for Samaria.

Mesha-Stele-tourism. The Moabite king Mesha's stele (discovered 1868) gives a Moabite account of struggling against Omri and Ahab that has fascinated archaeologists for over a century. Some treatments lift this archaeological celebrity into a positive Omri rehabilitation: he must have been an impressive king if Mesha had to fight him so hard. The stele is genuinely interesting as confirmation of biblical narrative; it does not change the canonical verdict. The doctrinal point about Omri is unchanged by the size of the army Moab had to raise to resist him: he led Israel in the way of Jeroboam son of Nebat, and the LORD's witness against him stands.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Omri (H6018); uncertain meaning, possibly "life" or "servant of Yahweh." Sixth king of Israel (c. 885-874 BC); founder of the Omride dynasty; builder of Samaria.
